title: One purpose, many payers: City money and private grants for the same kind of work
question: Where the City and several private funders pay one organization for the same stated purpose in the same year, do the amounts fit inside what it says it spent?
finding: 367 organization-years across 135 organizations pair City payments ($883.7 million) with grants from two or more private funders ($235.8 million) for the same kind of work. In none of them do the City payments and private grants for that one purpose exceed the organization's whole reported spending for the tax year ending that year: on this test the totals fit (the tightest is Episcopal Community Svcs of SF Inc in 2022, where housing and homelessness money from both sides is 94% of spending). Counting every City payment and every private grant found, whatever the purpose, 3 of these organization-years exceed reported spending (1 of them already listed, for City payments alone, in the 'Do the books agree?' screens): Counterpulse 2021 ($1.4 million against $968,014 spent); The SF Housing Accelerator Fund 2023 ($5.6 million against $4.9 million spent).
how: Each private grant's stated purpose and each City contract's title (or, where the title fits no theme, the paying department's name) were sorted into twelve plain themes by keyword. The first theme that fits is used, in this order: child care and early education (child care, preschool, early care, early childhood, early learning, early education, infant, toddler); meals and food (food, meal, nutrition, pantry, hunger, grocery); job training (workforce, job, employment, apprentice, career); mental health and drug treatment (mental health, behavioral health, substance, addiction, overdose, harm reduction, sober, detox); legal help and immigration (legal, immigrant, immigration, asylum, citizenship, eviction defense); violence prevention and victims (violence, victim, trafficking); seniors (senior, older adult, elder, aging); small business (small business, entrepreneur, merchant, microenterprise); housing and homelessness (homeless, shelter, housing, unhoused, navigation center, rehousing); health care (clinic, health care, medical, HIV, AIDS, dental, primary care); arts and culture (art, arts, artist, theater, music, dance, museum, culture, cultural, film, festival, exhibit, symphony, opera, ballet); youth programs (youth, after school, summer camp, summer program, summer learning, tutor, mentor, literacy). Grants given only for 'general support' fit no theme and are left out. A row is one organization, one year and one theme with $50,000 or more of City payments and $50,000 or more from at least two private funders. The year is the City fiscal year, and the calendar year in which the funders' and the organization's tax periods end. The later columns set the money against the total contributions and total expenses on the organization's own return for that year. Rows are ranked by the smaller of the City and private amounts.
limits: A City contract may not cover a programme's full cost. A shared theme is not a shared cost; only the grant budgets would show whether one cost was charged twice. The three calendars differ (City fiscal year, funder tax year, recipient tax year), City payments under a contract can be for work in an earlier year, and a grant paid in one year can be spent over several or go into a building or a loan fund that is not counted as spending, so a single year can look overfull. A fiscal sponsor's return covers many projects, and a grant to an organization that works in several counties may be for work elsewhere. Keywords misfile some purposes. State grants on the same themes are in the State grants screen (linked in the last column) and are not repeated here.
